title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the same candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We revise the manuscript to (1) compact provenance into a concise archival-reference paragraph; (2) add a formal, compact binary pass/fail scoring rule (with a concrete example drawn from archived scoring artifacts); and (3) insert a nearest-work comparison matrix that contrasts the present shared-generation paired design against the closest prior executable-benchmark and tool-augmentation studies. We preserve all preregistered analyses and archived evidence and discuss construct/external validity and design recommendations for follow-ups where repair can be meaningfully exercised.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can map operator intent to concrete device configuration commands, promising productivity gains for NetOps. However, syntactically plausible outputs may violate stateful or workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing hazardous make-before-break uplink switchover) that only closed-loop execution exposes. Prior work therefore recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment. Evaluating guarded pipelines requires executable tests that detect semantic and stateful failures beyond token- or syntax-level correctness.

We executed a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) designed to isolate the marginal effect of an executable validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The confirmatory research question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? Using a shared-initial-candidate paired design (one generator output per task scored under both conditions) removes generator-induced variance and measures validator/repair influence directly. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N=120) that isolates validator/repair marginal effects; (2) condensed, artifact-referenced provenance to enable reproducible verification; (3) a compact formal definition of the binary scoring rule used for the confirmatory McNemar test with an explicit example from archived scoring JSON; and (4) a nearest-work comparison matrix contrasting our design choices with the closest prior studies.
sections.related_work:
Two complementary strands motivate and contextualize this study. First, executable-benchmark and closed-loop emulation efforts show that textual or syntactic correctness is insufficient for safe enactment: closed-loop emulation surfaces sequencing and stateful errors (make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, ordered-operation requirements) that simple syntactic checks miss (see NetConfArena and related executable-benchmark work). Second, tool-augmented agent architectures and bounded-autonomy guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model, generate→validate→repair) are proposed and prototyped as practical safety measures.

Nearest-work comparison (compact):
- Protogeros et al. (Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair, arXiv:2604.22513): generator-focused benchmark that measures repair quality across model outputs; differs from our study by not using a shared-generation paired design and by focusing on multi-call repair behavior across generator draws.
- Liu et al. (NetConfArena, arXiv:2608.23179): an executable, closed-loop benchmark that evaluates agent behavior in emulated networks; closest in using emulation but typically compares independent generator draws and multi-agent flows rather than isolating validator marginal effects with shared-generation pairing.
- Zhou et al. (MeshAgent, DOI:10.1145/3771567): system for reliable management with LLMs emphasizing operational integration; differs by focusing on system architecture and operational workflow rather than a preregistered paired causal test of a validator subsystem.
- Tang et al. (Lightyear, DOI:10.1145/3603269.3604842): verification-scaling work that advances verification tooling; differs by focusing on verification scalability rather than guarded generate→validate→repair experimental isolation.
- Augé et al. (Aether, arXiv:2604.18233): digital-twin + agentic-validator concepts; similar architectural motives but evaluated in broader agent scenarios rather than the tightly controlled paired test here.

Key distinctions of the present study: (i) shared-initial-candidate paired design that holds the generator output fixed across conditions to directly measure validator/repair marginal effects; (ii) strict preregistration and deterministic reconciliation artifacts; (iii) a repair budget limited to ≤1 repair per guarded episode to study bounded repair influence. These differences are summarized to clarify how our mechanistic question complements generator-focused evaluations in the cited literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and experimental design. The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) prior to execution. The design is a paired-binary confirmatory experiment with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks each. We used a shared-generation stage: for each pair the generator produced one shared initial candidate (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) which was then scored under baseline (LLM-only suggestion semantics) and guarded (executable validator ± repair) conditions. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline with an exact two-sided McNemar test (alpha = 0.05) and a bootstrap-percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). The preregistration specified exclusion rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses.

Validator, task encoding, and scoring. Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, intent, required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable emulator/validator that enforces structured workflow policies (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break). The validator emits a structured validator_trace including validation_before, validation_after, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, and a repair_applied flag. Preregistered repair semantics invoked at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count > 0; repair prompts and provider traces are archived when generated. In this run validator.violation_count = 0 across all guarded episodes and repair_applied = false everywhere.

Compact provenance paragraph (condensed archival references). To support reproducible verification while avoiding provenance bloat in the main narrative, all primary execution and analysis artifacts required to reproduce the reported accounting are archived and checksummed. Representative primary artifacts (available in the archived evidence bundle) include: execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap parameters and seed). The full execution manifest and the complete artifact hash manifest are archived with the study; readers and auditors can consult those files for end-to-end verification. (Reviewer-requested long provenance inventories and checksums are preserved in the archived execution manifest rather than expanded in the main text.)

Formal binary scoring rule (compact, explicit). The confirmatory McNemar test uses a per-pair binary pass/fail label determined by the deterministic scorer/validator outputs. The rule implemented for scoring each episode is: an episode is a PASS (label=1) iff all of the following hold: (a) scoring_status == "COMPLETED"; (b) score == 1 (scorer reason code indicating VALID_CONFIGURATION); and (c) validator_trace.validation_after.valid == true. Otherwise the episode is a FAIL (label=0). This rule maps the deterministic validator’s structured verdict and the scorer’s intent-level check into the binary outcome used in the paired contingency table. Concrete example (archived artifact): execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json contains scoring_status = "COMPLETED", score = 1, score_reason_code = "VALID_CONFIGURATION", and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; therefore the episode is scored PASS (label=1) under the formal rule. A fail example (not observed in this run) would be validator_trace.validation_after.valid == false or score == 0; the archived scoring JSON schema records the fields used by this deterministic mapping.

Instrumentation and contamination controls. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets (container image checksums + deterministic seeds) between tasks and recorded provider-call audits and duplicate-output detectors. Contamination heuristics (duplicate-output detection, cross-condition cache-key reuse) were applied and none triggered exclusions in this run. Deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm planned vs completed episodes and provider-call accounting.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions: planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Condition-level summaries record baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0, guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rates = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table records n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes; no repair-provider artifacts exist because the guard never triggered repair.

Per-topology outcomes. The preregistered deterministic partition yielded 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology counts (from archived scoring artifacts and analysis/condition_summary.csv): Edge: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Core: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40; Leaf–spine: baseline 40/40, guarded 40/40.

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring artifacts (for example execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) show normalized_response equals normalized_reference_answer; parsed_command_count equals required_command_count from the task payload; validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true; validator_trace.repair_applied = false; validator_id = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator_version = 5.0. These artifacts corroborate the formal binary mapping and the per-episode PASS labels used in the confirmatory table.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The shared-generation paired design isolates validator/repair marginal effects by holding generator outputs fixed across conditions. Under the declared prompt strategy and the supplied synthetic task bank the generator produced valid candidates for every tested task; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The observed McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling. This outcome does not contradict claims that validators can reduce semantic failures in other settings; it indicates that, for this curated task bank and generator/prompt setup, generator errors did not arise.

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but risks under-exercising repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen task bank. Based on archived task-manifest difficulty metadata (dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, difficulty level) and the absence of repairs we recommend for future confirmatory runs aimed at measuring repair utility: (1) permit independent generator draws per condition (or prespecified paired perturbation arms) to increase discordant pairs arising from generator variance; (2) concentrate confirmatory power on 'very_hard' tasks or high-dependency tasks to increase error incidence; (3) include exploratory arms with expanded repair budgets to measure repair convergence and cost.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: strong (deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audit logs, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces). Construct validity: limited by synthetic task payload encodings and the validator’s modeled policy set; some production failure modes (vendor-specific behaviors, partial observability) may not be captured. External validity: constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions (baseline failure ≈0.40) were violated by observed baseline = 0.00, rendering the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
